prompt: What is behaviour-driven development, at bottom?
hint: The lesson starts by naming the usual picture as wrong.

choices.text: Agreeing on examples of the behaviour before the code
choices.why: Right. Examples in words the business would sign, settled before code exists; a tool may turn them into tests afterwards.

choices.text: Writing the tests in English sentences with Cucumber
choices.why: That is the tool, and the lesson calls it the wrong picture: a team can install Cucumber and practise none of BDD.

choices.text: Testing through the screens instead of through classes
choices.why: BDD says nothing about which layer is driven. The bookshop's scenarios call the HTTP API and have no screen at all.

choices.text: Testers writing the tests once the developers have finished
choices.why: That is the order BDD reverses: the tester is one of the three people in the conversation that comes first.

prompt: In the conversation about stock, the tester asks what happens when there are no copies at all. Why is that question worth asking there rather than later?

choices.text: Because zero stock breaks the database's CHECK constraint
choices.why: The constraint is `stock >= 0`, so zero is a legal value; the outline's second row sets it and the scenario passes.

choices.text: There it costs one sentence; after release, a fix and a deployment
choices.why: Right. A bug report, a fix and a deployment, against one answer from the business person while everybody is in the room.

choices.text: Because Cucumber cannot add a scenario once the code exists
choices.why: Scenarios are added at any time; the lesson adds a step after the code and Cucumber simply reports it as undefined.

choices.text: Because only the tester may write examples
choices.why: Three people write them together, and the business person answered this one.

prompt: What makes a feature file "living documentation", where a requirements document is not?

choices.text: It is written in plain language that non-developers can read
choices.why: So is a good requirements document. Plain language is what makes it readable, not what keeps it true.

choices.text: It is kept in the repository beside the code
choices.why: A document can sit in the repository and still go stale; being near the code does not check it.

choices.text: It is generated from the code every time the build runs
choices.why: It is the other way round: people write it, and the code is checked against it.

choices.text: It runs, and fails the build when the code stops agreeing
choices.why: Right. A file that passed this morning says what the software does today, not what somebody once wanted.

prompt: When do the steps under `Background:` run?

choices.text: Once, before the first scenario of the file
choices.why: That would leave later scenarios with whatever the first one left behind; the background is repeated instead.

choices.text: Before every scenario of the file, outline rows included
choices.why: Right. As if they were written at the top of each one, which is why every scenario gets a token of its own.

choices.text: Once per run, before any feature file
choices.why: A background belongs to its file and runs for that file's scenarios, each time.

choices.text: Only before the scenarios whose steps mention the same customer
choices.why: Cucumber never reads the meaning of a sentence; the background runs before all of them.

prompt: The bookshop's `ordering.feature` runs once. How many times is the step `Given the customer "ana" has signed in` executed?
hint: Count the scenarios after the outline is expanded.

prompt: Which of these steps is written declaratively?

choices.text: When she sends a POST to /orders with bookId 4 and quantity 2
choices.why: That is how the step is carried out, in HTTP terms: it has to be rewritten whenever the API changes shape.

choices.text: Then the response body has totalCents equal to 6400
choices.why: A JSON field name is the API's vocabulary, not the shop's; a renamed field breaks the sentence.

choices.text: When she orders 2 copies of "Persuasion"
choices.why: Right. It says what happens in the shop's words, and only the method behind it knows about URLs and JSON.

choices.text: Given the book table has stock 5 in the row titled Persuasion
choices.why: That is the arrangement as SQL would put it. The lesson's step does write the table, but the sentence does not say so.

prompt: Match each Gherkin keyword to what the lines it starts are for.

pairs.right: the rows that fill an outline's holes

right_distractors: the steps every scenario of the file runs first

prompt: The step `Given the customer "ana" has signed in` matches `"the customer {string} has signed in"`. What does the method's `name` parameter receive?

choices.text: `"ana"`, with the quotes
choices.why: The quotes mark where the text starts and ends in the sentence; `{string}` drops them.

choices.text: `ana`, without the quotes
choices.why: Right. `{string}` matches quoted text and passes what is inside the quotes.

choices.text: the whole sentence after `Given`
choices.why: Only the part matched by the hole is passed; the literal words around it just have to be there.

choices.text: nothing until the parameter is annotated with `@Param`
choices.why: There is no such annotation in Cucumber: values go to the parameters in the order of the holes.

prompt: In a Cucumber expression, the hole that matches a whole number such as 6 and hands the method an `int` is written `{___}`.
hint: It has the name of the Java type.

prompt: The glue has `@Given("the shop has {int} copies of {string}")` and nothing else matching those words. A feature file says `Then the shop has 5 copies of "Frankenstein"`. What does Cucumber do with that line?
hint: What does Cucumber compare a step against?

choices.text: Reports it as undefined, since no `@Then` matches it
choices.why: The annotation's keyword plays no part in matching; a method found by its words is found whatever word starts the line.

choices.text: Refuses the file as malformed Gherkin before running anything
choices.why: The file is well formed: `Then` followed by any text is a valid step.

choices.text: Runs the `@Given` method with 5 and Frankenstein
choices.why: Right. The keyword is for the reader. That is also why one sentence cannot both arrange and check: it reaches the same method either way.

choices.text: Skips it, because a `Then` may not change state
choices.why: Cucumber has no rule about what a step may do; it would run the method, which writes the stock.

prompt: The bookshop's `Given the shop has … copies of …` writes the stock instead of checking that it is what the seed put there. Which reasons does the lesson give or show for that? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: A test class that ran earlier may have handed over its context and database
choices.why: Right. In the full `verify`, CucumberIT ran in the context BooksApiIT had left, orders and all.

choices.text: Nothing rolls the database back between scenarios
choices.why: Right. Every write was committed as it happened, so each scenario finds what the one before left.

choices.text: No seeded book has 0 copies, so the outline's second row needs a write
choices.why: Right. A step that only checked could not express that example at all.

choices.text: Cucumber refuses assertions inside a `Given` method
choices.why: It refuses nothing of the kind: the bookshop's `Given` asserts that exactly one row changed.

choices.text: A step definition cannot call the HTTP API before the `When`
choices.why: The background signs in over HTTP before every `When`; any step may call the API.

prompt: Two methods in the glue have patterns that both match the same sentence. What happens when a scenario reaches it?

choices.text: Cucumber runs whichever method it found first on the classpath
choices.why: That would make the result depend on class loading order; Cucumber refuses to guess.

choices.text: Cucumber runs both of them, one after the other
choices.why: A step is one action or one check, and running two would hide which one the author meant.

choices.text: It is an error, and Cucumber names both methods
choices.why: Right. Every sentence has to match exactly one method across all of the glue.

choices.text: Cucumber picks the method whose annotation keyword matches the line's
choices.why: The keyword is not part of the match, so it cannot break a tie either.

prompt: Why is the suite class called `CucumberIT` rather than `CucumberTest`?

choices.text: Cucumber only discovers suites whose names end in IT
choices.why: Cucumber does not discover the suite at all; Maven's plugins pick test classes by name, and the engine is chosen by `@IncludeEngines`.

choices.text: So Failsafe runs it in `mvn verify`
choices.why: Right. Lesson 19's split: `*Test` for Surefire in `mvn test`, `*IT` for Failsafe in `mvn verify`.

choices.text: Because a JUnit suite must not end in Test
choices.why: JUnit has no such rule; the name only matters to the Maven plugin that decides which classes to run.

choices.text: So that Surefire runs it in `mvn test`, before the unit tests
choices.why: That is what a `*Test` name would do, and it would put a database and a whole application into the fast tests.

prompt: Match each dependency added in this lesson to what it brings.
hint: The leftover one is the job of something imported, not of a dependency.

pairs.right: the glue created as Spring beans
an engine that finds .feature files and runs scenarios
@Suite, the class that says what to run

right_distractors: one version for every Cucumber module

prompt: What does `"features"` in `@SelectPackages("features")` name?

choices.text: The Java package that holds the step definitions
choices.why: That is the glue, `com.example.bookshop.acceptance`, set by its own configuration parameter.

choices.text: A classpath package holding the .feature files
choices.why: Right. `src/test/resources/features/` is copied there by the build, and the report says `classpath:features/ordering.feature`.

choices.text: The text after `Feature:` in every file that should run
choices.why: Cucumber prints a feature's name but never selects by it here; the selection is by location.

choices.text: A tag that every scenario to run must carry
choices.why: Tags start with `@` in the feature file and are filtered by another parameter; this file has none.

prompt: In the full `mvn verify`, three integration test classes each started a PostgreSQL container and `CucumberIT` started none. Why?
hint: Compare CucumberSpringConfiguration's annotations with lesson 20's test class.

choices.text: Spring reused BooksApiIT's cached context
choices.why: Right. Same annotations, same cache key: the context, its port and its database came from BooksApiIT.

choices.text: Cucumber scenarios use the student's own PostgreSQL from lesson 9
choices.why: The `test` profile and `@Import(TestcontainersConfiguration.class)` are on the configuration class; nothing points at the local server.

choices.text: Testcontainers is switched off inside a JUnit suite
choices.why: Nothing switches it off; run on its own, CucumberIT starts a container like the others.

choices.text: Cucumber starts the container later, when a step first needs the database
choices.why: The container is a bean of the Spring context, started with it; no step starts one.

prompt: Put in order what happens for the outline's second row, from the moment Cucumber reaches it.
hint: The hook runs before the background.
items: Cucumber creates a new OrderingSteps, with its beans from the cached context
the @Before hook points REST Assured at the server's port
the background signs ana in and keeps her token
the Given writes 0 copies of Persuasion
the When asks for 2 copies and keeps the answer
the Thens check the 409 and the stock

prompt: A scenario reaches a step no method matches. What happens with Cucumber 8?

choices.text: The scenario errors, the build fails, and a snippet is printed
choices.why: Right. `UndefinedStepException`, with the skeleton of the missing method in its message.

choices.text: The step is skipped and the scenario passes on the others
choices.why: That would let a sentence that runs nothing read as a check that holds, and Cucumber does not allow it.

choices.text: It passes with a warning unless strict mode is switched on
choices.why: Older versions had a strict switch; Cucumber 8 has no setting that lets an undefined step pass.

choices.text: Cucumber writes the missing method into src/test/java
choices.why: It prints a snippet for a person to paste and finish; it never edits the source.

prompt: In a scenario, the third step fails. What happens to the fourth?

choices.text: It runs anyway, so that every failure in the scenario is reported
choices.why: Every later step assumed the earlier ones held, so its result would mean nothing.

choices.text: The whole feature file stops, and no later scenario runs
choices.why: The other scenarios ran and passed in the lesson's run; only the failing one stops.

choices.text: It is skipped
choices.why: Right: the curved arrow in the report. Cucumber runs nothing else in a scenario once a step has failed.

choices.text: It runs once the failing step has been retried
choices.why: Cucumber does not retry a step; a failure is reported as it happened.

prompt: A team has two hundred Cucumber scenarios. Only developers have ever opened the feature files, and the steps are 4,000 lines of glue. Following the lesson, what is the sound advice?

choices.text: Keep them all, since living documentation costs nothing once it is written
choices.why: It costs the indirection, the vocabulary and the mending, and here nobody collects the benefit.

choices.text: Rewrite the steps imperatively, so the developers see the HTTP calls
choices.why: That moves the code into the sentences and keeps both layers; the cost goes up, not down.

choices.text: Delete the scenarios and rely on the unit tests' coverage instead
choices.why: That throws away the examples, which are the part of BDD the lesson says is not optional.

choices.text: Keep the agreed examples as well-named plain tests, drop the sentences
choices.why: Right. The examples are the part worth keeping; the sentences only pay when somebody who reads no Java reads them.

prompt: A product owner edits only the feature file, changing `she orders 2 copies of "Persuasion"` to `she buys 2 copies of "Persuasion"`. The Java is untouched. Which statements are true of the next `mvn verify`? Choose every one that applies.
hint: What joins a sentence to a method?

choices.text: The renamed step is undefined, and the build fails
choices.why: Right. No pattern matches the new words, and an undefined step is an error.

choices.text: `sheOrders` still exists and is simply not called by that line
choices.why: Right. Nothing ties a method to a sentence except the text; the method waits for a sentence that matches it.

choices.text: Cucumber runs `sheOrders`, the closest match to the new words
choices.why: Matching is exact against the pattern; there is no nearest match.

choices.text: Only the report changes; the build stays green
choices.why: An undefined step fails the build, which is what makes a detached sentence impossible to miss.

prompt: A new rule arrives: a customer may not order more than ten copies of one book. Put the work in the order BDD with Cucumber does it.
items: agree examples of the rule with the business and a tester
write the examples as scenarios in the feature file
run them and read the snippets for the undefined steps
write the step definitions that call the API
change the application until the scenarios pass

prompt: A feature file has a background of 2 steps, one scenario of 4 steps, and one scenario outline of 4 steps with 3 rows in its Examples table. In a run where everything passes, how many steps are executed in total?
hint: First count the scenarios, then remember what runs before each one.
